en: Looking nowhere about him,
Having heard Ismail's words,
Sparing his life not at all,
They beat the drums
And went to block the narrow road.
Thus your mother
Was now waylaid by the orphan.
With seventy champions behind,
Semetey came burning with rage.
Let us leave this here,
Upon the saddle-shaped ridge
She stood unable to find peace,
Your mother Kanykei.
Let us begin to tell of her.
Your dear mother Kanykei
Was a blessed soul.
A voice was heard, its owner unseen:
Upon your sister-in-law's shoulder
There was a naked child.
Of torment and of sorrow
That child gave warning.
Gripping her ear and murmuring,
Then her child
Whispered to her:
'Oh, Kanykei, poor soul,
Dip your hands in water,
Perform your hands' ablution.
Put your feet in water,
Perform your feet's ablution.
That dear bird, the wild duck—
From the plain whence it does not return,
Wild with racing horses,
You will die before your appointed death
At the hands of the child from your womb.
If Taitoru comes first,
You will see your orphan.
If Taitoru falls behind,
You will die before your time.
Unsaved from suffering,
You will face the Last Judgment.
If Taitoru comes first,
God has granted your wish.
If this horse falls behind,
Give up your hope of life.
With seventy champions beside him,
Your orphan comes in a frenzy,
Their swords gleaming,
To cut off your head,
His champions come in a frenzy.
The khan's command is a grievous thing;
Now force has come upon you.
If this bay horse falls behind,
You will braid the hair down your back.
Through the champions given orders,
You will die before your time.
When seven wolves rend one sheep,
Will they leave its carcass?
If seventy champions and Semetey
Beat you, will they leave your corpse?
Your kin has become your enemy;
Your anguish is shut inside you.
He chose his spear and swung it;
Your own brother Ismail
Turned him to evil and sent him.
He will slaughter your life like a fly,
Will drain your strength.
Semetey, left by your khan Manas,
Comes to shed your blood.
Desired today, gone tomorrow—
Such is this shit of a world.
Your orphan, left by the warrior,
Will heap live coals upon your head.
To separate you and save you,
Look, your Kyrgyz people are not here.
You have no support to lean upon,
No stronghold where you can take shelter.
Racing your horse without foreknowledge,
You have thus come to nothing.'
When she heard this news,
Her heart burned into embers.
That blessed, passionate woman's
Beloved people were not here.
She had no support to lean upon,
She grieved sorely on that road;
Her renowned Argyn people were not here.
Her rib bones came apart,
The tears streamed from her eyes,
Her poor heart was torn apart.
By the son born of herself
It seemed that she would die.
A dark day fell upon her.
Upon your sister-in-law's head
Seventy afflictions fell at once.
Unless the one Creator God
Himself came to her aid,
Upon your sister-in-law's head
Utter calamity had fallen.
Unable to stand, crying out in tears,
She despaired of her very life.
Finding not a fly's worth of recourse,
Her heart was sorely torn,
The tears poured from her eyes.
Her heart was sorely torn.
By the son born of herself
It seemed that she would die.
Upon the winding plain,
She cried out in terrible fear
Of the child born from her womb.
Unable to turn Akborchuk's head,
Unable to stop her tears,
From her pitiful quail-like eyes,
From the mother you have seen,
The tears fell drop by drop.
From her dear currant-black eyes
The tears streamed a whip's length.
‘That dear bird, the wild duck—
From the plain whence it does not return,
Wild with racing horses,
Will I die before my time
At the hands of the child from my womb?
That dear bird called the little bustard—
From the plain from which it flies away,
Wild with racing horses,
I am to die an unshriven death, alas,
At the hands of the child I bore my lord.
I ran like a hunting hound.
Distress came upon me,
I fled here from Talas.
In a world that brought me hardship,
Cutting his twig,
Performing his rite,
The son born of my own body
I gave to Ismail.
My darling camel-calf, left by the noble one,
Has not yet learned to put on his shirt.
That I, the mad, bewildered woman,
Am his mother, he does not yet know.
His thoughts are elsewhere:
Semetey is another Sart's son.
He will seize me on my road, alas,
And despite my pleas will spare me nothing.
My sorrow-laden life
He will slaughter as a sacrifice, alas!
My thick, girth-like hair down my back
I am to braid, alas.
Wild with racing horses,
By the orphan left by my khan
I am to die, alas!
The decree ordained by God
I am to witness, alas.
My own morning star has turned against me;
I am to die, alas!
I could not escape, O God,
The sorrow and care within my heart.
Crazed with racing horses,
How shall I escape
The child born from my breast?!
Though I wail from morning till night,
My wretched life cannot escape the written decree.
Who can flee and escape,
When the time to collect their debt arrives,
From these eighteen thousand worlds?
The dug grave will take them in,
The black earth will enclose them.'
Unable to keep her courage firm,
'Well, if my death has come, I shall die.
The line that God has drawn
Has reached my head; I shall face it!
Not only I—all sorts of peoples have passed,
The holy elders have all passed.
Not only I—so many warriors have passed,
All sorts of lions have passed,
Twelve ages have passed together,
Many saints have passed.
I have no strength to leap away,
No means to turn my thoughts aside.
To say, "Oh, sister-in-law, do not weep,"
To speak words of counsel,
My dear people are not here.'
Saying so, she girded herself
And took courage now.
For death and torment,
Your mother now girded herself.
Back when her fierce champion died,
When your sister-in-law met disaster,
When Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
The vast wealth left by the blood-shedder
Divided into equal shares for all,
When your mourning sister-in-law Kanykei
Suffered terrible torment,
The ten treasuries of riches
Abyke, Kobosh, two villains,
Chiybyt, Kochkor, four villains,
Adybai, Kolbai, six villains,
Divided into equal shares for all.
Left to face it alone,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Bereft of her blood-shedding hero,
At thirty-two years of age,
When King Manas died,
When your sister-in-law met calamity,
All the treasure, the countless riches—
The forty companions left by Manas
Swarmed in to look upon them.
When they turned their steeds toward her,
The woman sitting widowed
They struck and beat till she writhed.
When they devised their cruel scheme,
When they slashed her breast open,
Dragging her like a kok-boru carcass,
When the woman dressed in mourning
They dragged down along the Talas,
When they carried out their scheme,
The thick flesh of her thigh
The wretched, overgrown dog
Struck again and again that day.
The forty companions, fearing no ancestral spirit,
Drew their bows like rain
And shot their arrows like hail.
When your dear sister-in-law Kanykei
Suffered cruel humiliation,
The leopard-woman Kanykei,
Unable to stay weeping in sorrow,
Such humiliation as no one should see
Had she not endured?
The white saddlebag brought from the Alash—
Had your sorrowful sister-in-law not borne it?
The blaze-faced horses on the hills,
Fine steeds mixed with racehorses—
Had she no complaint to God?
Her little son upon her back,
All her own kin her enemies,
Surviving simply because she had not died,
With Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
And the forty companions, your sister-in-law
Fought alone.
A merciless struggle
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Had she not fought?
Your champion's great telescope,
Keeping it as a memento,
In the fold of her wraparound skirt
She stitched it fast, securely hidden,
To pass it to her champion Semetey,
Weeping bitterly to the one God,
His father's telescope
She had set aside for Semetey,
Bound and stitched it up again.
In the fold of her wraparound skirt,
Your valiant mother Kanykei
Had hidden it securely for safekeeping.
The telescope she had brought,
From her skirt's fold,
Wailing and weeping piercingly,
Your champion's telescope
She now took out, sobbing,
